lines: First make each specified pair into its own two-person block.
Arrange all resulting units, but remove the unit arrangements in which the two pair-blocks touch; each pair still has two internal orders.
The calculation is {equation}, so {answer} rows satisfy both restrictions.
Compress the specified pair and trio into two separate blocks.
Count all unit arrangements and subtract those where the two formed blocks are adjacent, then restore the internal orders of both blocks.
Using {equation}, the required number of arrangements is {answer}.
Treat the specified group as one block, while the named outsider remains a separate unit.
From all unit arrangements, remove the cases in which that outsider is immediately before or after the block, and then arrange the people inside the block.
Begin by keeping the required pair together as one unit.
From those pair-together arrangements, subtract the cases in which the separate trio also forms a complete consecutive block.
Therefore {equation}, so {answer} arrangements meet the mixed condition.
The phrase at least one pair is not together excludes only the arrangements in which both specified pairs form blocks at the same time.
Count every unrestricted row and subtract the simultaneous two-block arrangements, including the internal reversals of both pairs.
That calculation is {equation}, giving {answer} acceptable arrangements.
For each allowed value of \(n\), form the two pair-blocks and exclude arrangements where those two blocks are adjacent.
Exactly one candidate produces the target {target}; for that candidate the verified calculation is {equation}.
Hence the original number of people is {answer}.
